prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. I was trudging along a muddy path in a column of downcast men on the blackened outskirts of New York, the twilight dingy and ruined, the future without hope as we marched along in our soiled, proletarian rags. To my left was Mayakovsky, head shaved, and next to him his friend with gray beard and dark cap. "You've got to admit," Mayakovsky was saying, "that this is a pretty good way to write a poem." "Yes," I said, "the momentum is sustained by our walking forward, the desolate landscape seeps into every word, and you're free to say anything you want." "That's because we're inside the poem," he said, "not outside." Puddles of oily water gleamed dully beneath the low clouds. "That's why my poems were so big: there's more room inside." The hard line of his jaw flexed and the men dispersed. I followed his friend behind a wall to hear the poem go on in the lecture the friend was giving on history, but no, the real poem had finished. I went back to the spot where the poem had finished. Vladimir had left the poem.

I must confess that these events occurred purely within a dream I experienced yesterday evening. I found myself sludging through mire, part of a line of demoralized men traversing the charred borderlands of New York City. Clad in filthy, working-class garments, we pressed onward beneath a decayed, murky dusk that offered no promise for tomorrow. 

Positioned to my left was a bald Mayakovsky, accompanied by a friend who wore a dark hat and had a silver beard. The poet remarked that generating verse in this fashion was remarkably effective. I concurred, noting that our physical progression maintained the rhythm, the grim surroundings infused every utterance, and we possessed absolute freedom of speech. He clarified that this was possible because we were situated within the literary piece itself, rather than viewing it from the exterior. 

Under a low, overcast sky, slick pools of murky water cast a faint shimmer. He added that the immense scale of his own writings was due to this phenomenon, as an interior space inherently affords much greater capacity. 

His rigid jaw tightened, prompting the crowd to scatter. I tracked his companion past a wall, expecting the verse to persist through a historical lecture the man was delivering; however, the genuine piece had already reached its end. Upon returning to the exact location of its conclusion, I realized that Vladimir was no longer present in the work.

I found myself submerged in a dream composed of ash, iron, and silence. I was marching along the outer fringes of New York, a desolate wasteland where the grand silhouette of the metropolis dissolved into jagged ruins, shattered concrete, and rusted steel. The sky hung low, heavy and bruised, threatening a rain that never fell. Surrounding me was a procession of downcast men, their heads bowed against a biting wind, their shuffling footsteps creating a slow, somber cadence against the broken earth.

As we pressed deeper into this bleak landscape, I realized the figure walking beside me was the Russian poet Vladimir Mayakovsky. He towered over the marchers, a colossal presence with broad shoulders squared against the gray horizon. Even in the gloom, his eyes burned with a fierce, restless intensity, and his heavy strides seemed to dictate the very tempo of our movement.

Without turning to look at me, Mayakovsky spoke, his voice deep and booming, echoing across the barren expanse. He explained that we were not merely wandering through a wasteland; we were actively writing and experiencing a poem from the inside out. The desolate environment around us was not a cemetery of the past, but the essential raw material for the work. He gestured toward the skeletal remains of factories and the vast, empty horizon, explaining that destruction clears the canvas, creating an infinite spatial freedom for the imagination. We were the meter, the rhythm, and the living breath of a verse forged from ruin. 

Just as the poetry of our march seemed to reach a powerful, unspoken crescendo, the surreal vision shattered. The thick atmosphere fractured, and the crowd of men abruptly dispersed, drifting away like mist in the wind. Mayakovsky turned toward the vast emptiness, took a few decisive strides, and vanished into the gray expanse. The poem ceased mid-phrase, leaving me stranded on the edge of consciousness, waking to the quiet residual echo of his voice.
outputs.L4:
The landscape of the dream was vast, stripped bare of ornamentation, and stretched out beneath a heavy, iron-grey sky. It was a desolate terrain of cracked earth, dust, and infinite horizon—a blank expanse waiting for form. Beside me marched Vladimir Mayakovsky. He did not merely walk; he cut through the space, his broad shoulders squared against an invisible wind, his jaw set, his heavy boots striking the ground in a fierce, metronomic cadence that seemed to shake the very foundation of the dream. 

As we pushed forward into the wasteland, our conversation turned to the nature of artistic composition. I spoke of the frustration of standing before the page, of trying to capture a vision from the outside—measuring lines, shaping stanzas, and carefully sculpting imagery as a stonemason might carve a block of marble from a distance. 

Mayakovsky scoffed, a sound like gravel turning in a cement mixer, and gestured wildly at the empty sky. 

"That is the fatal error of the timid!" he boomed, his voice reverberating across the tundra. "You treat the poem as an object in a gallery, something to be inspected, measured, and judged from a safe distance. You stand outside the burning house and try to paint the flames! To write a real poem, you must leap through the front door. You must build the architecture while you are burning inside it."

He argued that true creation demands a shift in dimension: one must step off the shore of analytical contemplation and submerge oneself completely into the current of the work. As we marched, the stark landscape around us began to shift, taking on the subtle geometry of syntax and sound. The ground beneath our feet became the pulse of meter; the wind taking shape around us became the breath of a voice striving for utterance. 

Inhabiting the poem from within, I realized, radically alters the artist's relation to the work. When standing outside, one is constrained by caution, paralyzed by the fear of error, and limited by cold, intellect-driven logic. But from the inside, the poem grants an immense and exhilarating scale. The walls of structure and form no longer feel like a cage; instead, they become a engine of velocity. You are no longer merely writing the rhythm—you are propelled by it. The room expands; the sky opens; the momentum of the words carries the writer forward with a terrifying, liberating force. Freedom, Mayakovsky insisted, is not found in the absence of form, but in the total, fearless surrender to its internal push.

As the dream began to dissolve—the grey horizon fragmenting into the dim light of my waking room—the poet’s final lesson lingered like the echo of his footsteps. External analysis, dissection, and distant craftsmanship may produce a clean, sterile arrangement of words, but they cannot give birth to living art. True poetry cannot be observed from a distance; it exists only in the act of living within its walls, riding its momentum, and braving the fire of active immersion.
outputs.L5:
**The Tapestry of All New York**

There is a distinct, undeniable frequency at which the metropolis vibrates. From the first light of dawn reflecting off the sleek glass of Midtown skyscrapers to the quiet midnight hum of tree-lined Brooklyn streets, **all** of **New York** seems to move to a rhythm that is entirely its own. 

It is a world built on relentless evolution. Every morning brings a **new** perspective, a **new** ambition, and a **new** story unfolding on a standard city block. Here, historic brownstones stand in the shadows of cutting-edge architectural wonders, proving that while the city respects its past, it is forever leaning toward tomorrow. It is a place where every corner promises a fresh discovery—a hidden coffee shop, a pop-up art gallery, or a quiet park bench overlooking the river.

What makes the experience so unforgettable, however, is its sheer scope. **All** walks of life converge in this concrete expanse. In a single subway ride, you can hear a dozen languages spoken, smell the rich aromas of global cuisines, and catch glimpses of the dreamers, workers, and creators who give the city its soul. From the tranquil green pathways of Central Park to the electrifying neon heartbeat of Times Square, **all** aspects of the human spirit find a stage here.

Ultimately, **New York** is more than just a place on a map; it is an energy, an attitude, and a living, breathing phenomenon. No matter where you come from or how long you stay, once you have felt its unyielding pulse, a piece of **all** that **New York** represents stays with you forever.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short story about having a dream where you walk through a ruined New York alongside Vladimir Mayakovsky.
counterfactuals.output:
The sky was the color of a fresh bruise, stretched tight over the shattered grid of Manhattan. I stood at the corner of 42nd and Broadway, but there were no lights, no yellow cabs, no rushing tide of coats and briefcases. There was only the sound of salt wind rushing through the hollow eye sockets of skyscrapers. 

Beside me stood a giant. 

He was a mountain of a man in a dark, heavy overcoat, his jaw set like a anvil. A damp cigarette dangled from his lower lip, unlit, yet a thin wisp of silver smoke trailed from it anyway. 

Vladimir Mayakovsky. 

He did not look at me; he looked up, where the top half of the Chrysler Building lay sheared off, resting like a discarded knight’s helmet in the overgrown ruins of Bryant Park. 

"I told them," he rumbled. His voice wasn't a whisper—even in a dream, Mayakovsky was incapable of whispering. It was a cello played with a iron bow, a brass horn echoing down an empty alleyway. "I told them in twenty-five. I saw the steel. I saw the elevators plunging like brass guilt. I said: *Your soul is a machine, but machines rust.*"

We walked down Fifth Avenue. Nature had begun its violent reclamation. Oaks squeezed through the asphalt; ivy draped over the rusted chassis of buses like velvet shrouds. The air smelled of damp earth and ozone, of sea salt and old paper.

"You wrote a poem about the Brooklyn Bridge," I said, my voice sounding thin and small against the vast, silent canyon of iron. 

"I praised the rivets!" Vladimir roared, striking his broad chest with a fist. "I bowed to the engineers! I sang to the triumph of human muscle over distance! And look at it now." 

He gestured with a long, sweeping arm toward the East River. We walked until the asphalt gave way to torn cables and shattered granite. 

The Brooklyn Bridge hung in the mist like a broken harp. Its great suspension cables were snapped, dangling into the black water below, humming softly when the wind caught them. 

Mayakovsky stepped up to the jagged edge of the masonry, his heavy boots stirring a cloud of centuries-old dust. He threw back his head. His dark eyes caught the dim, violet light filtering through the clouds. He looked magnificent and tragic—a constructivist statue left out in the rain.

"Is this the end of the world, Vladimir Vlyadmirovich?" I asked.

He turned to me, a sudden, fiercely brilliant smile flashing across his face, breaking the hard gloom of his features. 

"No, comrade!" he bellowed into the abyss. "It is just the intermission! The set must be torn down so the next act can begin! Look at it—no bankers! No stock tickers drowning the heart in paper ribbons! Just iron, returning to the dirt! Just the sky, finally allowed to touch the river!"

He stepped closer to the edge, spreading his arms wide as if to embrace the dead metropolis. He began to recite, his voice falling in jagged, stepped rhythms, shaking the dust from the fallen beams:

*"I shall leap!*
*I shall leap over the sun,*
*my heart bleeding brass,*
*my lungs full of thunder!"*

The sound swelled, vibrating in the marrow of my bones. The shattered city seemed to ring like a cathedral bell under the weight of his voice. The fog tore open. The sky above us didn't bring daylight, but a blinding, yellow flare—a sun made entirely of burning copper.

The heat of it washed over my face. The sound of his voice grew so loud it ceased to be words and became pure vibration, rattling my teeth, shaking the pavement beneath my feet until it dissolved into nothingness.

I woke up. 

Outside my window, real cars hummed on a real street. The morning sun was pale and weak. But on my tongue, I could still taste the bitter, electric tang of ozone and salt—and in the distance, somewhere behind the radiator's hiss, a brass horn was still blowing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective prose passage that begins with the narrator admitting a dream. In the dream, the narrator should be marching in rags through a bleak, desolate landscape with Mayakovsky, discussing the idea of being "inside" a poem versus outside of it.
counterfactuals.output:
I have to admit to the dream, if only because it haunts my waking fingers like the film of cold grease. Last night, I was marching through a dead landscape—a vast, hollow expanse of bruised mud, slag, and shattered iron under a sky the color of a dirty nickel—and Vladimir Mayakovsky was marching beside me. 

We were both clad in rags, heavy with frozen slush, flapping against our shins like wet wings. He was as enormous as his legacy, a towering monument of a man shaved down by starvation, his jaw set like an anvil, his boots biting into the tundra with the brassy, uneven rhythm of a steam press. 

"The mistake," he bellowed, his voice heavy as wet coal, turning to face the bitter gale, "is thinking you can ever step back to view the canvas."

We were talking, as the dead and the desperate do, about the geography of the poem. 

"To be outside the poem," Mayakovsky spat, his breath blooming in the frigid air like white smoke, "is a luxury for the faint-hearted. It means sitting in a warm kitchen with a cup of tea, measuring the lines with a little wooden ruler. You are safe there. But you are merely a spectator to your own extinction."

"And inside?" I asked, pulling my rags tighter, my teeth chattering against the biting wind. "What is it like inside?"

He stopped, his fierce, hollowed eyes locking onto mine, the wind whipping his dark hair into a crown of thorns. "Inside, there is no shelter from the metaphor. The sky isn't *like* lead; it *is* lead, and it is crushing your skull. You do not analyze the blood; you supply the ink. Inside the poem, the walls are made of your own ribs, the syntax is a cage, and there are no doors. You burn, but at least you are the fire."

I woke up before we reached whatever horizon we were marching toward, but the frost has not entirely left my chest. 

Standing now by my window, watching the neat, unrhymed traffic crawl down the paved street, I am struck by a quiet, terrible revelation. I have spent most of my life striving to stay outside—keeping my distance, maintaining my composure, analyzing the world from behind a barrier of safe, quiet prose. But looking at my clean, warm hands, I wonder if the comfort I have preserved is just a comfortable kind of numbness. I wonder if, in my terror of being consumed by the verse, I have condemned myself to be nothing more than a ghost, standing outside the glass, watching a life I was too afraid to actually inhabit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of surreal micro-fiction exploring the relationship between movement, landscape, and poetic scale, featuring Russian Futurist poets in a dark, modern setting?
counterfactuals.output:
Under the eight-lane flyover of a midnight metropolis, Vladimir Mayakovsky adjusted his lapels against the smog-rain. He was forty feet tall, but only when he moved. The moment he paused, he collapsed back into the cramped geometry of an ordinary man standing under a flickering neon advertisement for synthetic sleep.

Beside him, Velimir Khlebnikov sat on a wet jersey barrier, peeling the noise of passing maglev trains into prime-numbered vowels. He caught a transrational syllable of *Zaum* between his fingers—it glowed like a dying moth, possessing the exact mass of a vanished mountain range. 

"The city’s meter is dragging," Mayakovsky rumbled. His voice produced no sound, only kinetic load; it bent the overpass’s steel girders into jagged, aggressive trochees. He took a single, violent stride forward, and thirty blocks of damp asphalt folded like a paper fan beneath his heel. Distance was no longer a spatial truth, merely a function of lung capacity and stride.

Aleksei Kruchenykh stepped out from the dark alcove of an automated teller machine, his cheek painted with a black lightning bolt. *"Dyr bul shchyl,"* he hissed into the smog. 

The sound shattered the modern architecture. Where the consonants struck the road, the asphalt tore open to reveal a ancient, silent steppe humming beneath the fiber-optic cables. 

Mayakovsky reached up, snatched a handful of high-voltage static from a skyward transformer, and forged it into a single, blinding iamb. He pitched it down the expressway. The landscape warped around the verb’s trajectory—skyscrapers shrank into a row of fifty-story periods, while their three shadows expanded to swallow the horizon, moving infinitely faster than the light that cast them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dreamlike, melancholic paragraph where a writer walks with Soviet poets on the muddy outskirts of a city, reflecting on momentum and how poems end.
counterfactuals.output: We trudged through the black, thawing melt of the city’s edge, their heavy wool coats smelling faintly of damp tobacco and abandoned apartments, the gray geometry of the pre-fab towers dissolving behind us like salt in wet air. Beside me walked the ghosts of the Soviet line—heads bowed against a sky the color of bruised zinc, their boots dragging a slow, trochaic cadence through the ankle-deep mud that fought for every step. In that dim, syrupy dusk, I understood that a poem’s momentum is rarely a leap toward illumination, but rather an inescapable physics: a heavy sled pushed over the brow of a hill, gathering a dark, terrible velocity only to exhaust itself against the soft terrain of its own making. We reached the point where the rutted road simply gave up into cold reeds and standing water, and I realized how a stanza truly dies—not with the sharp click of a lock or a grand gesture, but like this urban fringe, where the rhythm falters beneath its own weight, leaving a final, shivering phrase to hang suspended over the mire, waiting for the silence to rise up and swallow the last trailing syllable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Start a paragraph with "All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night." and write a surreal vignette where Vladimir Mayakovsky explains why his poems were so big.
counterfactuals.output: All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. Vladimir Mayakovsky was crouching on my nightstand, six feet eight inches of iron jaw and yellow silk shirt, using a pocketknife to carve a slice out of the yellow moon that floated in my teacup. The room smelled of wet asphalt, steam engines, and raw lung power. When I asked him—my voice sounding like a faint whistle against his presence—why his verses were always so enormous, so terrifyingly, violently huge, he spat a spark of burning tobacco onto my carpet and roared, though he was only whispering. "Do you think a man with a heart the size of a locomotive depot can play a toy flute?" he grumbled, unclipping his ribs like the doors of a furnace to show me a glowing brass piston pumping in his chest. "I tried to write a quiet poem once. A little thing, tiny as a flea! I put it in my pocket, but by midnight it had consumed my trousers, swallowed the streetlamp outside, and grown arms long enough to punch the sky in the throat. You don't understand—the twentieth century was born screaming and completely deaf! If I hadn't built my lines like steel fire escapes, if I hadn't smashed my verbs into gargantuan dynamite bricks, my voice would have been drowned out by the rustling of tea leaves and the shuffling of old men's slippers." He stood up, his head vanishing through my bedroom ceiling into a sky made of red banners and shattered clocks, his voice booming down from the clouds: "My poems weren't big because I wanted them to be; they were big because the world was too small to hold my grief, so I had to push the walls out!"
